description: We are an Argentine team interested in space medicine and autonomous health tools for deep-space crews. We combine software engineering (TypeScript, image analysis), UX design and life sciences. During this hackathon we built Lynceus, an on-board first read of eye changes in astronauts (SANS), based on NASA’s published definitions and thresholds, with a transparent analysis that shows its own uncertainty.
summary:
Lynceus is a web app that gives astronauts an on-board first read of Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), an eye condition that shows up in about 70% of long-duration crew members and usually causes no symptoms. It guides the astronaut through a short eye check-up on screen. After each retinal OCT exam, it tells them whether the back of each eye changed compared with their own pre-flight exam, by how much, how certain that result is, and which monitoring step comes next, using NASA’s published definitions and thresholds. The same result is prepared as a report for the flight surgeon on Earth, who confirms it and decides.

Our prototype simulates the tomograph used on the International Space Station, producing fictional exams in its real export format, and analyzes them with a real, deterministic image-analysis engine that runs on the device. As missions go farther from Earth, communication delays grow and crews will need to understand their own health with more autonomy. All data in the demo are simulated; it is not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
Lynceus guides an astronaut through a complete eye check-up for SANS, alone and without medical training:

  1. Start: choose the crew member and flight day; see which check is due.
  2. Vision tests, done by the person in front of the screen: a symptom questionnaire, near visual acuity (after calibrating the real screen size with a card) and an Amsler grid.
  3. OCT capture of each eye. If the image is not good enough, the system asks for a retake, up to three times; then it says “I can’t measure this eye today” instead of guessing.
  4. Analysis and result, for each eye: whether it changed since before the flight, by how much (with a range), how likely the change is to be real, the level and the next monitoring step.
  5. History: the evolution of each eye across the mission, with thresholds.
  6. Medical conference: a downloadable report for the flight surgeon and the questions the astronaut wants to ask.

HOW IT WORKS

  • A virtual instrument imitates the Heidelberg Spectralis OCT2 used on the ISS: 48 radial scans centered on the optic nerve, with noise, shadows and capture failures, written in the device’s real .vol export format.
  • An analysis engine reads that file, checks its quality, finds the retinal surface and Bruch’s membrane with a graph-search method (Chiu et al., 2010), locates the optic nerve opening and measures retinal thickness around it, as NASA defines it. It also measures the waviness of Bruch’s membrane as an indicator of new folds.
  • Each measurement is compared with the same eye’s pre-flight exam and given an error range. NASA’s thresholds set the level: more than 19.4 µm is a first sign (NASA rounds it to 20 µm) and 55 µm or more is clinically concerning. Acute vision symptoms trigger contact with the surgeon regardless of the image.
  • The same input always gives the same output, and every number shows its unit, its range, how it was obtained and its source.
  • An optional assistant answers questions about the result and SANS from a fixed, cited knowledge base. It cannot change the level, diagnose or recommend medication.

BENEFITS

  • The astronaut understands their own status right after the exam, instead of waiting for specialists on Earth.
  • The flight surgeon receives a traceable report: what was measured, how well, with what uncertainty, and which tests were done or skipped.
  • The analysis works without a connection, which matters as communication delays grow toward the Moon and Mars.

INTENDED IMPACT
Farther from Earth, crews will need to understand their own health with more autonomy. Lynceus is a traceable prototype to study an on-board first read of SANS, always with the flight surgeon confirming and deciding. Next steps: test on real, independent OCT images reviewed by experts, calibrate the error ranges, and test with crew-like users.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE
We chose one problem and took it all the way through, instead of a dashboard with many indicators. Each eye is compared with its own pre-flight exam, and the result comes with its uncertainty, its level and a next step, in one inspectable path from image to report. The analysis is real code measuring pixels; every number shows how it was obtained.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED
The astronaut works alone and may have worse near vision, so nothing depends on color alone and text is large with high contrast. We keep the human in charge: the flight surgeon confirms. We separated measurement, rules and AI explanation, so the measurement works even if the assistant is unavailable. We state our limits: all data are simulated, the error model is provisional, and the tool does not diagnose or estimate intracranial pressure.

WHAT IS REAL AND WHAT IS SIMULATED
The four crew members and their images are fictional and labelled as simulated on every screen and report. The vision tests, the image analysis, the rules and the report are real. We tested the engine on 621 simulated captures with known true values; the fitted error model did not meet the criteria we set before the final test, so the app keeps a provisional error model and says so. It is not a medical device and is not validated on people.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES
TypeScript throughout; React and Vite for the web app; Vitest for more than 600 automated tests; our own CSS and charts, with no component library; Vercel for hosting and one serverless function; the Anthropic API (Claude Haiku 5.5) for the optional assistant. Interface in English and Spanish.
